q: Pictured: handrail. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Gabay” is the vernacular for handrail. Origin: Tagalog gabay “guide”. A handrail guides you up the stairs.

q: Pictured: open stringer. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Hardinera” is the vernacular for open stringer. Borrowed from Spanish jardinera (Philippine Spanish hardinera), “garden planter”. How it came to mean an open stringer isn't clear. Memory hook: an open stair is airy like a garden.

q: Pictured: astragal. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Batidura” is the vernacular for astragal. Likely from Spanish batir “to beat, strike”, the strip a door strikes against. Don't confuse Batidura (astragal, fillet) with Batidora (door fillet).

q: Pictured: baluster. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Barandilla / Barandillas” is the vernacular for baluster. Origin: Spanish barandilla “railing”, from baranda.

q: Pictured: moulding. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Muldura” is the vernacular for moulding. Origin: Spanish moldura “moulding”.

q: Pictured: landing. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Mesa, Mesita” is the vernacular for landing. Origin: Spanish mesa “table” and mesita “little table”. A landing is a small flat platform in the stair.

q: Pictured: tread. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Baytang” is the vernacular for tread. Origin: native Filipino baitang “step”.

q: Pictured: stair. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Hagdan” is the vernacular for stair. Origin: native Tagalog word for stairs.

q: Pictured: closed stringer. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Madre de Eskalera / Escalera” is the vernacular for closed stringer. Madre is Spanish “mother”: the main member that carries the steps, like a mother carrying her children. Escalera is Spanish “stair, ladder”.

q: Pictured: door fillet (astragal). Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Batidora” is the vernacular for door fillet (astragal). Likely from Spanish batir “to beat, strike”, the strip a door strikes against. Don't confuse Batidora (door fillet) with Batidura (astragal, fillet).

q: Pictured: quarter round. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Media Cana” is the vernacular for quarter round. Origin: Spanish media caña “half cane”. The moulding has the rounded profile of a cut reed.
